author: Robert Frick, Kiplinger's Personal Finance
title: Investing: Investing like Warren Buffett
text:
Business 's moves -- his record is unrivaled.
Fortunately, his holding company, Berkshire Hathaway (symbol BRK-B), reveals what's in its portfolio four times a year. Here are some of Buffett's latest noteworthy moves -- along with recommendations of whether you should follow his lead.
Current favorite: Berkshire boosted its stake in APPLE (AAPL) by 23 percent to $28 billion. That makes it Berkshire's biggest position, topping the $27.8 billion stake in his longtime favorite, Wells Fargo .
Recommendation: Buy. Wall Street analysts, on average, expect Apple to earn $11.55 a share in the fiscal year ending in September, up 25 percent from fiscal 2017 and more than double that year's 10.8 percent earnings growth rate, says research firm S&P Global Market Intelligence. Buy on dips, however; the stock price was recently close to the average of analysts' price targets of $191 by mid-2019.
Banking on banks: Buffett's love of the financial sector is long-standing and only strengthening. Berkshire boosted its position in BANK OF NEW YORK MELLON (BK) by 21 percent, bringing its total stake to $3.3 billion. The economic climate is good for financials. The Federal Reserve raised short-term interest rates three times in 2017 and is on track to raise another three times in 2018, which helps banks generate a better return on their cash reserves.
Recommendation: Buy. Even with a positive trend in interest rates, bank stocks remain how Buffett likes them: cheap.
Planting the seed: Seed and pesticide company MONSANTO (MON) has been a fast-growing holding for Berkshire, but still not a large position. Monsanto's shares aren't cheap.
Recommendation: Hold. Buffett isn't betting the farm on Monsanto, nor should you.
Still on board: Berkshire unloaded 1 million shares of AMERICAN AIRLINES (AAL), a minor repositioning, says Robert Johnson, CEO of the American College of Financial Services. Berkshire still owns shares of SOUTHWEST AIRLINES (LUV), DELTA AIR LINES (DAL) and UNITED CONTINENTAL HOLDINGS (UAL). Buffett wasn't a fan of airlines in the 1990s, but bargain share prices have likely "changed his mind," says Johnson.
Recommendation: Buy. Several of Buffett's airline stocks sport price-earnings ratios that are less than 10, including American, Delta and United, all at about 9.
Going in a new direction: Berkshire Hathaway cut its stake in GENERAL MOTORS (GM) by 16 percent. The automaker now represents a minuscule 1 percent of Berkshire's portfolio.
Recommendation: Sell. Although the stock's valuation is tempting, the company's growth prospects are dim.
Finally giving up: Shares of IBM have gone nowhere since Berkshire started accumulating them in early 2011. The rest of the market doubled in value. Buffett unloaded 35 million IBM shares in the latest quarter.
Recommendation: Sell. The company's revenue has fallen in each of the past six years. IBM isn't a top player in mobile computing or corporate cloud computing, two of the explosive sources of tech growth.
